meanings.GV.OC-01: Cybersecurity priorities should support what the organization exists to deliver, including the services whose disruption would threaten that mission.
meanings.GV.OC-02: Understand what internal and external stakeholders expect from cybersecurity so risk decisions reflect their needs and responsibilities.
meanings.GV.OC-03: Identify the obligations that shape cybersecurity decisions and assign responsibility for keeping those obligations understood.
meanings.GV.OC-04: Understand which services other organizations or people rely on you to provide, and the consequences if those services fail.
meanings.GV.OC-05: Understand the outside services and capabilities your own operations depend on, including concentration and disruption risks.
meanings.GV.RM-01: Leadership and stakeholders need a shared view of what cybersecurity risk management is intended to achieve.
meanings.GV.RM-02: Make clear how much risk the organization is willing to take and when exposure exceeds acceptable boundaries.
meanings.GV.RM-03: Cybersecurity exposure should inform the organization's wider business-risk decisions rather than remain a separate technical list.
meanings.GV.RM-04: Define how the organization chooses among reducing, accepting, avoiding or otherwise responding to cybersecurity risk.
meanings.GV.RM-05: Risk information needs a reliable route to the people who can act on it, including relevant suppliers and partners.
meanings.GV.RM-06: Use a consistent way to describe, assess and prioritize risks so different teams can compare decisions meaningfully.
meanings.GV.RM-07: Consider opportunities as well as downside risks, such as how improved cybersecurity can enable a new service safely.
meanings.GV.RR-01: Leadership remains accountable for cybersecurity risk and for the culture that shapes how people manage it.
meanings.GV.RR-02: People need to know who owns each responsibility, who may decide and when issues must be escalated.
meanings.GV.RR-03: Provide people, time and resources appropriate to the cybersecurity risks and responsibilities the organization has accepted.
meanings.GV.RR-04: Hiring, role changes and departures should account for cybersecurity responsibilities and access-related risks.
meanings.GV.PO-01: Translate cybersecurity direction into policies that are communicated and applied within the organization.
meanings.GV.PO-02: Keep policy aligned with changes in risks, operations and obligations; an approved document can still become obsolete.
meanings.GV.OV-01: Review the results of the cybersecurity strategy and use them to adjust the organization's direction.
meanings.GV.OV-02: Check whether the strategy still covers the organization's important risks and requirements.
meanings.GV.OV-03: Evaluate how well risk management is working, not merely whether planned activities were marked complete.
meanings.GV.SC-01: Treat cybersecurity supply-chain risk as a managed program with agreed objectives and practices.
meanings.GV.SC-02: Make supplier-related security responsibilities clear inside the organization and with the relevant third parties.
meanings.GV.SC-03: Include supplier exposure in wider cybersecurity and business-risk management decisions.
meanings.GV.SC-04: Identify which suppliers matter most so assurance effort reflects their criticality and access.
meanings.GV.SC-05: Communicate and incorporate appropriate security expectations into supplier agreements.
meanings.GV.SC-06: Understand material supplier risks before committing to a relationship, rather than discovering them after adoption.
meanings.GV.SC-07: Manage supplier risk throughout the relationship as services, access and business conditions change.
meanings.GV.SC-08: Include relevant suppliers in incident preparation, response and recovery coordination.
meanings.GV.SC-09: Monitor whether supply-chain security practices are being performed and remain effective.
meanings.GV.SC-10: Plan for what happens when a supplier relationship ends, including data, access and continuing dependencies.
meanings.ID.AM-01: Know which hardware assets the organization manages so protection and ownership do not depend on guesswork.
meanings.ID.AM-02: Know which software, systems and services are used, including those delivered outside the organization's own infrastructure.
meanings.ID.AM-03: Understand how systems communicate and where information moves across network and organizational boundaries.
meanings.ID.AM-04: Maintain visibility of supplier-provided services and the business activities they support.
meanings.ID.AM-05: Prioritize assets according to their sensitivity and importance, rather than treating every asset as equally critical.
meanings.ID.AM-07: Know what important data exists and retain the context needed to identify, protect and manage it.
meanings.ID.AM-08: Manage assets throughout acquisition, use, change and disposal so protection does not end at deployment.
meanings.ID.RA-01: Identify weaknesses affecting assets and confirm which findings represent genuine exposure.
meanings.ID.RA-02: Obtain threat information relevant to the organization and make it available for risk decisions.
meanings.ID.RA-03: Identify plausible threats from both inside and outside the organization.
meanings.ID.RA-04: Consider how likely threat events are and what harm they could cause in the organization's context.
meanings.ID.RA-05: Combine threats, weaknesses and consequences into an understanding of exposure before selecting a response.
meanings.ID.RA-06: Choose risk responses, assign responsibility and track whether the response is carried out.
meanings.ID.RA-07: Understand and document how changes or exceptions affect risk before treating them as acceptable.
meanings.ID.RA-08: Provide a way to receive and act on reports of vulnerabilities affecting the organization.
meanings.ID.RA-09: Consider whether acquired hardware and software are authentic and trustworthy before relying on them.
meanings.ID.RA-10: Assess critical suppliers using the risks their products, services and access introduce.
meanings.ID.IM-01: Use assessments and evaluations to identify concrete improvements to cybersecurity practices.
meanings.ID.IM-02: Turn exercises and tests into improvements rather than stopping at a completed exercise record.
meanings.ID.IM-03: Capture lessons from routine operations and incidents and use them to improve practices.
meanings.ID.IM-04: Maintain usable plans for incidents and other cybersecurity events as the environment changes.
meanings.PR.AA-01: Manage identities and credentials through their lifecycle for people, services and devices.
meanings.PR.AA-02: Establish that an identity represents the intended person, service or device before connecting it to access credentials.
meanings.PR.AA-03: Verify identities appropriately before allowing people, services or hardware to access resources.
meanings.PR.AA-04: Protect identity claims exchanged between systems so an attacker cannot easily forge or misuse them.
meanings.PR.AA-05: Limit permissions to justified needs and review them as roles and circumstances change.
meanings.PR.AA-06: Control physical access in a way that reflects the risks to the assets and environment being protected.
meanings.PR.AT-01: Give the workforce the knowledge needed to carry out everyday activities with cybersecurity risks in mind.
meanings.PR.AT-02: People with specialized responsibilities need training appropriate to the security decisions and tasks they perform.
meanings.PR.DS-01: Protect stored information from unauthorized access, change or loss within its relevant environment.
meanings.PR.DS-02: Protect information while it moves between people, systems and organizations.
meanings.PR.DS-10: Protect information while applications and people actively process or use it.
meanings.PR.DS-11: Maintain protected backup copies and demonstrate that they can support recovery when needed.
meanings.PR.PS-01: Manage system configurations deliberately so approved security settings are established and maintained.
meanings.PR.PS-02: Maintain, replace and remove software with its security and support lifecycle in mind.
meanings.PR.PS-03: Maintain, replace and remove hardware before its condition or support status creates unmanaged risk.
meanings.PR.PS-04: Generate the logs needed to understand activity and support monitoring and investigation.
meanings.PR.PS-05: Prevent software that lacks authorization from being installed or executed within the assessed scope.
meanings.PR.PS-06: Include security in software development and maintain it as applications change.
meanings.PR.IR-01: Protect networks and environments against unauthorized access and adverse use.
meanings.PR.IR-02: Account for physical and environmental conditions that could disrupt or damage technology.
meanings.PR.IR-03: Use resilience mechanisms that allow important services to withstand adverse conditions.
meanings.PR.IR-04: Maintain enough capacity to support availability needs, including conditions that increase demand or reduce resources.
meanings.DE.CM-01: Observe network and service activity so potentially adverse events can be detected.
meanings.DE.CM-02: Monitor relevant physical conditions and access for events that could affect cybersecurity.
meanings.DE.CM-03: Monitor personnel activity and technology use for potentially adverse events within appropriate organizational boundaries.
meanings.DE.CM-06: Include relevant external service-provider activity in monitoring rather than assuming it is handled elsewhere.
meanings.DE.CM-09: Monitor the computing environments and information relevant to detecting adverse events.
meanings.DE.AE-02: Analyze detected events to understand whether they indicate a cybersecurity problem.
meanings.DE.AE-03: Combine information from multiple sources to reveal relationships that isolated alerts may miss.
meanings.DE.AE-04: Determine which systems, information and business activities an event may affect.
meanings.DE.AE-06: Get useful event information to the people and tools responsible for action.
meanings.DE.AE-07: Use relevant threat context to interpret detected activity and improve its analysis.
meanings.DE.AE-08: Use defined criteria to decide when an adverse event becomes an incident requiring response.
meanings.RS.MA-01: Carry out the incident response plan with coordination among the relevant internal and external parties.
meanings.RS.MA-02: Check incoming incident reports and determine which need action.
meanings.RS.MA-03: Classify incidents and prioritize them according to their consequences and urgency.
meanings.RS.MA-04: Escalate incidents when the situation needs additional authority, expertise or resources.
meanings.RS.MA-05: Use agreed conditions to decide when recovery activities should begin.
meanings.RS.AN-03: Investigate what happened and why so the response addresses causes as well as symptoms.
meanings.RS.AN-06: Record investigation actions so decisions and the sequence of work can be understood later.
meanings.RS.AN-07: Preserve relevant incident information and its origin so it remains useful and trustworthy.
meanings.RS.AN-08: Validate the scale of the incident as new information becomes available.
meanings.RS.CO-02: Notify the relevant stakeholders about an incident according to the organization's applicable obligations and plans.
meanings.RS.CO-03: Share incident information with designated parties through appropriate channels.
meanings.RS.MI-01: Limit an incident's spread and immediate impact while response work continues.
meanings.RS.MI-02: Remove the conditions sustaining the incident so normal operation can be restored safely.
meanings.RC.RP-01: Carry out the recovery plan when incident response determines that recovery should proceed.
meanings.RC.RP-02: Choose and sequence recovery actions according to the organization's priorities.
meanings.RC.RP-03: Check recovery assets before using them so restoration does not reintroduce the original problem.
meanings.RC.RP-04: Restore critical mission and business functions while accounting for remaining risks.
meanings.RC.RP-05: Confirm that restored systems operate correctly and safely before relying on them again.
meanings.RC.RP-06: Use defined conditions to close recovery and retain the supporting record of that decision.
meanings.RC.CO-03: Keep relevant stakeholders informed about recovery progress and remaining limitations.
meanings.RC.CO-04: Coordinate approved public recovery communications so external messages are accurate and consistent.

groups.GV.OC: Typical implementation connects mission, stakeholders, obligations and dependencies to a documented scope and accountable decision-makers. A scope statement should reflect real services and dependencies, not only an organization chart.
groups.GV.RM: Typical implementation records agreed objectives, decision boundaries and a consistent risk method, then uses them in actual business decisions and reporting.
groups.GV.RR: Typical implementation assigns named responsibilities and decision rights, communicates them and checks whether staffing and resources support those responsibilities.
groups.GV.PO: Typical implementation gives policy an owner, approval path and change triggers, then communicates the policy and checks how it is applied.
groups.GV.OV: Typical implementation uses management review of results, gaps and changing risks to decide adjustments and track follow-through.
groups.GV.SC: Typical implementation ties supplier criticality and access to due diligence, agreements, ongoing assurance and exit planning. The applicable activity depends on the relationship stage and this outcome.
groups.ID.AM: Typical implementation reconciles inventories and dependency information with actual operations, assigns owners and tracks lifecycle changes and exceptions.
groups.ID.RA: Typical implementation connects relevant threats and weaknesses to scoped impacts, accountable risk decisions and traceable response work.
groups.ID.IM: Typical implementation records lessons from assessments, exercises or operations, assigns improvements and checks whether the changes work.
groups.PR.AA: Typical implementation manages identity lifecycle, authenticates the relevant access paths and limits privileges. Check actual coverage, service identities, exceptions and timely removal rather than assuming one identity tool covers everything.
groups.PR.AT: Typical implementation assigns relevant training to the intended audience, tracks completion and checks whether people can apply it in their responsibilities.
groups.PR.DS: Depending on the data state, typical implementation combines access restrictions, encryption, integrity and recovery measures. Confirm scope and operating evidence rather than relying on a broad policy statement.
groups.PR.PS: Typical implementation connects approved settings and lifecycle processes to deployment, change records and checks of exceptions or failures.
groups.PR.IR: Typical implementation connects service resilience needs to architecture, environmental protection, capacity and tested recovery or continuity measures.
groups.DE.CM: Typical implementation defines monitored sources, checks coverage and health, and assigns responsibility for investigating detections.
groups.DE.AE: Typical implementation correlates relevant evidence, establishes event scope and routes decisions through clear incident criteria and escalation paths.
groups.RS.MA: Typical implementation connects incident plans to actual triage, priorities, coordination and decisions made during an incident or exercise.
groups.RS.AN: Typical implementation preserves investigation records, records decisions and revises the assessed cause and scope when new evidence arrives.
groups.RS.CO: Typical implementation identifies recipients, responsibilities and communication channels and retains an appropriate record of notifications and information shared.
groups.RS.MI: Typical implementation documents containment or eradication actions, their operational impact and how the result was checked.
groups.RC.RP: Typical implementation connects recovery priorities to trusted restoration assets, validation steps and a documented return-to-operation decision.
groups.RC.CO: Typical implementation assigns communication ownership, keeps stakeholders informed and coordinates any public updates with the recovery facts.
